explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. The text says God "…had no one greater to swear by…" so "…He swore by Himself…" (Hebrews 6:13). Nobody sits above Him, so He put His own name behind the promise. That's about as solid as a promise gets.
Close, but angels aren't who He swore by. The text says He "…had no one greater to swear by…" and angels are not greater than God. So "…He swore by Himself…" (Hebrews 6:13).
I get the thought, friend. Big sky, big oath, right? But the heavens aren't greater than God either. The text says He had no one greater, so "…He swore by Himself…" (Hebrews 6:13).

explanations.answer: Bless him and give him many descendants
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker! God said, "I will surely bless you and multiply your descendants." (Hebrews 6:14). Blessing and a whole lot of family. I think Abraham was going to need a bigger dinner table.

explanations.answer: Make him a priest in a great temple
explanations.explanation: Not this one, friend. The oath in this passage has nothing to do with a temple or priesthood for Abraham. God said, "I will surely bless you and multiply your descendants." (Hebrews 6:14).

explanations.answer: Give him silver and gold all his life
explanations.explanation: I see why you'd think so, baker, but silver and gold aren't in this oath. What God swore was, "I will surely bless you and multiply your descendants." (Hebrews 6:14). It's a promise about blessing and family.

That's the word, baker. "…after waiting patiently, obtained the promise." (Hebrews 6:15). Abraham didn't grab it early. He waited, and then he got it. I'd have been checking the oven every four seconds.

I'd be the restless one, friend, pacing the kitchen and peeking at the timer. But that's not what the text says about Abraham. It says he obtained the promise "…after waiting patiently…" (Hebrews 6:15).
Waiting can make a person steaming, I know. But the text doesn't describe Abraham that way. It says he obtained the promise "…after waiting patiently…" (Hebrews 6:15).

Right, baker. The writer says an oath "…serves as a confirmation to end all argument." (Hebrews 6:16). When someone swears by someone greater, the matter is settled. Picture a family debate over the last cookie finally ending. That's the idea.

Good guess, since oaths do feel like deal-makers. But the text gives a different job. The oath "…serves as a confirmation to end all argument." (Hebrews 6:16). It's about settling the argument, not trading.
Ha, that's the opposite, friend! The oath exists to shut the debate down. The text says it "…serves as a confirmation to end all argument." (Hebrews 6:16). No second round.

That's right, baker. God wanted to make "…the unchanging nature of His purpose very clear to the heirs of the promise…" (Hebrews 6:17). His purpose doesn't shift around. He guaranteed it with an oath so they could see it.
Not hidden, friend. The oath was meant to make the unchanging nature of His purpose "very clear" (Hebrews 6:17). Hiding is the opposite of what He was doing. The word is "unchanging."
I like gentle, baker, but that's not the word here. The text says God wanted to make "…the unchanging nature of His purpose very clear…" (Hebrews 6:17). It's about His purpose staying the same.

Yes, baker, you got it. The text says it is "…impossible for God to lie…" (Hebrews 6:18). God made a promise to Abraham and guaranteed it with an oath (Hebrews 6:13, 17). Those are the two unchangeable things. That's a solid base to stand on.
Good thought, friend, but rest isn't the word. The text says it is "…impossible for God to lie…" (Hebrews 6:18). That's why His promise and oath can be trusted.
Waiting was Abraham's job, baker, not what's impossible for God here. The text says "…it is impossible for God to lie…" (Hebrews 6:18). That's what makes the two unchangeable things so trustworthy.

That's right, baker. The text says that by these two unchangeable things, "…we who have fled to take hold of the hope set before us may be strongly encouraged." (Hebrews 6:18). Strong encouragement is what those two things give.

Not quite, friend. The text says it's true. By two unchangeable things, "…we who have fled to take hold of the hope set before us may be strongly encouraged." (Hebrews 6:18). Those who grab hold of that hope get real encouragement.
That's the one, baker. "We have this hope as an anchor for the soul, firm and secure." (Hebrews 6:19). An anchor that wobbled wouldn't be much use. This one holds.
Think about an anchor, friend. Light and quick would send the ship drifting right off! The text says the hope is "…firm and secure." (Hebrews 6:19).
Warm and bright sounds lovely, like fresh cookies out of the oven. But it's not how the writer describes the anchor. He says this hope is "…firm and secure." (Hebrews 6:19).
Yes, baker! Hebrews says "…Jesus our forerunner has entered on our behalf." (Hebrews 6:20). He went in first, for us. That's what a forerunner does.
Moses, Israel's leader (Exodus 3:10), is a big name, friend, but he's not the one here. The text says "…Jesus our forerunner has entered on our behalf." (Hebrews 6:20). Jesus went in ahead of us.
David, Israel's king (2 Samuel 5:3), is a great pick, baker, but he's not who the writer means. The text says "…Jesus our forerunner has entered on our behalf." (Hebrews 6:20). Jesus went in first.
Close, but that last part is the catch, friend. The text says Jesus "…has become a high priest forever in the order of Melchizedek." (Hebrews 6:20). It's forever, not for a set time.
That's right, baker. Jesus "…has become a high priest forever in the order of Melchizedek." (Hebrews 6:20). There's no end date on it. Forever means forever.
